messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
Property \(P\) means that every sequence \(F_n\) of nonempty closed subsets of \(M\) with \(F_{n+1}\subset F_n\) and \(\operatorname{diam} F_n\to 0\) has nonempty intersection.

Is completeness equivalent to property \(P\)?

If \(M\) is complete and \(F_n\) are nested nonempty closed with \(\operatorname{diam} F_n\to 0\), then one may choose \(x_n\) in \(F_n\), and \((x_n)\) is Cauchy because for \(m>n\), \(d(x_m,x_n)\le \operatorname{diam} F_n\).

Completeness gives a limit \(x\) in \(M\), and for every \(k\) the tail \(x_n\) with \(n\ge k\) lies in the closed set \(F_k\), so \(x\) lies in every \(F_k\) and the intersection is nonempty.

Does the converse follow by testing property \(P\) on tails of a Cauchy sequence?

If property \(P\) holds and \((x_n)\) is Cauchy, then the sets \(F_n=\overline{\{x_k\mid k\ge n\}}\) are nonempty closed, nested, and have diameters tending to \(0\) because the sequence is Cauchy, so property \(P\) yields a point \(x\) in the intersection.

For every \(\epsilon>0\) there exists \(n\) with \(\operatorname{diam} F_n<\epsilon\), and then \(x\) and \(x_n\) lie in \(F_n\), so \(d(x,x_n)<\epsilon\), hence \(x_n\) converges to \(x\).

Have both implications now been proved?

Yes, the nested-closed-sets property characterizes completeness in metric spaces.
